name: Tretinoin + microneedling stack
lead: The tretinoin plus microneedling stack is a skin-care combination discussed in appearance forums that pairs a topical retinoid (tretinoin) with microneedling, usually with a derma roller or derma stamp. People use it to smooth acne scars and rough texture, even out tone and reduce the look of ageing, with the idea that the retinoid and the needling each prompt the skin to renew itself.[1][2][3]

Each part has its own record. Wikipedia describes topical tretinoin as the most extensively studied retinoid for photoageing, with improvement usually taking weeks to months, and reports that it was developed for acne at the University of Pennsylvania in the 1960s and approved by the FDA for acne in 1971.[1] Dermatology guidelines make strong recommendations for topical retinoids in acne.[4] Microneedling, also called collagen induction therapy, is described as having been used for scarring and acne.[2]

Looksmax.org users talk about both tools in skinmaxxing threads, including a post describing alternating tretinoin nights with a derma stamp, while others report irritation or dark marks from tretinoin.[5][6] No published trial has tested the two together.

angle.text: Users combine a nightly retinoid with periodic microneedling hoping to soften acne scars, refine texture and reduce signs of ageing faster than either alone. The pairing is a forum-built routine rather than a studied protocol.

paras: Tretinoin (all-trans retinoic acid) is a retinoid applied as a cream, gel or lotion for acne and used for photoageing. It binds retinoic acid receptors in skin cells, which normalises follicle keratinisation and lowers inflammation in acne.[1] It is prescription-only in the US, UK, EU and Australia.[1]

Wikipedia lists redness, peeling, swelling and increased sun sensitivity as typical topical adverse effects and states that oral use in pregnancy is contraindicated.[1] The 2024 American Academy of Dermatology acne guideline strongly recommends topical retinoids, and a JAMA review covers their role among acne treatments.[4][7] Controlled trials of topical tretinoin on photoaged skin date to the 1980s.[8][9]

Microneedling repeatedly punctures the skin with tiny sterile needles; Wikipedia lists scarring and acne among its uses and notes it is sometimes paired with platelet-rich plasma, with efficacy of such combinations described as pending scientific study.[2] Health authorities have issued warnings, including a 2024 CDC report of HIV diagnoses linked to one spa's facial services, that concern infection control when such services are done by untrained providers.[2]

Forum users describe using tretinoin on some nights and a derma stamp or roller on others, and one thread title lays out a tretinoin night, a urea-cream night and a weekly stamp session over two months.[6] Posters argue that retinoid-driven renewal and needling-driven collagen remodelling complement one another. Specific schedules vary by poster and are not reproduced here.
Dermatology references on each component do not describe how they interact, and the effect on irritation when both are used has not been characterised in published studies.[1][2]

No studies found of tretinoin combined with microneedling. Studies exist on topical tretinoin alone for photoageing and acne, and microneedling combinations with platelet-rich plasma have been studied in split-face scar trials.[1][2][4][8][9]

Threads on looksmax.org include a user reporting dark spots around the mouth and a damaged skin barrier after starting a high-concentration tretinoin product, and others reporting worse acne or irritation.[5] Users in Australia discuss the prescription requirement for tretinoin.[10] Wikipedia notes irritation and sun sensitivity as the main topical effects of tretinoin.[1]

timeline.event: Controlled trial of topical tretinoin for photoaged skin published in the Journal of the American Academy of Dermatology.[9]
FDA approves microsphere tretinoin gel (Retin-A Micro).[1]

lore.intro: Tretinoin is a staple of looksmax.org skinmaxxing talk, and derma rolling is discussed as a companion step for scars and texture.[5][6][11]

claims.claim: Tretinoin and microneedling together improve scars and texture more than either alone
claims.believers: Users who alternate the two say each triggers collagen renewal by a different route, so the combination should resurface faster.[6]
claims.experts: No published study has tested the combination; tretinoin has a large photoageing literature and microneedling has scar studies of its own.[1][2]

claims.claim: Tretinoin improves acne and skin tone
claims.believers: Posters describe it as effective for acne and skin colour.[12]
claims.experts: The AAD guideline strongly recommends topical retinoids for acne, and Wikipedia describes it as effective in diverse patient groups.[4][1]

claims.claim: Tretinoin can cause irritation or dark marks if misused
claims.believers: One user reports barrier damage and dark spots after a strong product, and others report purging or worse acne.[5]
claims.experts: Wikipedia lists redness, peeling and sun sensitivity as topical adverse effects.[1]

card.summary: A forum protocol pairing prescription tretinoin with microneedling for scars and texture; each part has evidence, the combination has none found.
card.note: Tretinoin is Rx-only; both parts can irritate skin; no combination trials found.

quick.overview:
This stack combines a topical retinoid, tretinoin, with microneedling, usually at home with a roller, for scars, texture and aging signs.

Tretinoin is well studied for acne and photoaging and microneedling has been used for scarring, but no trial of the two together was found.
quick.mechanism: Tretinoin is a retinoid that acts on skin cell turnover and collagen over weeks to months. Microneedling makes controlled punctures intended to stimulate repair.
quick.risks: Tretinoin commonly causes irritation and sun sensitivity and is prescription-only in many countries. Microneedling carries infection concerns when done without proper hygiene.
